claim: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide.
source: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) being the most common subtype (Bray et al., 2018; Herbst et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bray et al., 2018 and Herbst et al., 2018

claim: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common subtype of lung cancer.
source: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) being the most common subtype (Bray et al., 2018; Herbst et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bray et al., 2018 and Herbst et al., 2018

claim: Activating mutations in the kinase domain of EGFR are present in about 10% to 40% of NSCLC patients.
source: Activating mutations in the kinase domain of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) are present in about 10% to 40% of NSCLC patients, most frequently in-frame deletions in exon 19 (ex19 del) and a missense arginine-to-leucine mutation at codon 858 (L858R) (Sharma et al., 2007; Pao and Chmielecki, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sharma et al., 2007 and Pao and Chmielecki, 2010

claim: The most frequent EGFR mutations in NSCLC are in-frame deletions in exon 19 (ex19 del) and a missense arginine-to-leucine mutation at codon 858 (L858R).
source: Activating mutations in the kinase domain of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) are present in about 10% to 40% of NSCLC patients, most frequently in-frame deletions in exon 19 (ex19 del) and a missense arginine-to-leucine mutation at codon 858 (L858R) (Sharma et al., 2007; Pao and Chmielecki, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sharma et al., 2007 and Pao and Chmielecki, 2010

claim: EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) such as erlotinib and gefitinib have provided therapeutic breakthrough and achieved clinical success.
source: The approval and use of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as erlotinib and gefitinib, have provided therapeutic breakthrough and achieved clinical success (Kobayashi et al., 2005; Rosell et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kobayashi et al., 2005 and Rosell et al., 2012

claim: The responses of EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients to EGFR TKIs are rarely complete with variable duration.
source: However, the responses of EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients to EGFR TKIs are rarely complete with variable duration (Kobayashi et al., 2005; Rosell et al., 2012), suggesting that other factors could modulate the dependency of mutant EGFR and thus influencing EGFR TKI efficacy.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kobayashi et al., 2005 and Rosell et al., 2012

claim: Acquired resistance to EGFR TKIs inevitably develops, leading to disease progression in almost all patients.
source: Moreover, acquired resistance inevitably develops, leading to disease progression in almost all patients (Pao and Chmielecki, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pao and Chmielecki, 2010

claim: Secondary EGFR T790M mutation accounts for about half of relapsed tumours with acquired resistance to EGFR TKIs.
source: Secondary EGFR on-target mutations, most frequently T790M mutation, account for about half of relapsed tumours with acquired resistance (Kobayashi et al., 2005; Pao et al., 2005; Sequist et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kobayashi et al., 2005, Pao et al., 2005, and Sequist et al., 2011

claim: Resistance to EGFR TKIs can result from reactivation of PI3K-AKT and RAS-MEK-ERK pathways.
source: Resistance can also result from reactivation of key downstream signaling pathways originally inhibited by EGFR TKIs, such as PI3K-AKT and RAS-MEK-ERK pathways (Chong and Jänne, 2013; Niederst and Engelman, 2013; Camidge et al., 2014; Rotow and Bivona, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chong and Jänne, 2013; Niederst and Engelman, 2013; Camidge et al., 2014; Rotow and Bivona, 2017

claim: Resistance to EGFR TKIs has been associated with amplification or activation of MET, HER2, FGFR and AXL.
source: For instance, resistance has been associated with amplification or activation of MET, HER2, FGFR and AXL, as well as PIK3CA mutation or loss of PTEN (Engelman et al., 2006; Engelman et al., 2007; Sos et al., 2009; Takezawa et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012; Ware et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engelman et al., 2006; Engelman et al., 2007; Sos et al., 2009; Takezawa et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012; Ware et al., 2013

claim: Resistance to EGFR TKIs has been associated with PIK3CA mutation or loss of PTEN.
source: For instance, resistance has been associated with amplification or activation of MET, HER2, FGFR and AXL, as well as PIK3CA mutation or loss of PTEN (Engelman et al., 2006; Engelman et al., 2007; Sos et al., 2009; Takezawa et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012; Ware et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Engelman et al., 2006; Engelman et al., 2007; Sos et al., 2009; Takezawa et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012; Ware et al., 2013

claim: Activation of NF-kB and YAP signaling pathways confers resistance to EGFR TKIs.
source: Moreover, activation of NF-kB and YAP signaling pathways also confers resistance to EGFR TKIs (Bivona et al., 2011; Hsu et al., 2016; Chaib et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bivona et al., 2011; Hsu et al., 2016; Chaib et al., 2017

claim: Histological transformation from NSCLC to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) has been reported in relapsed tumors after EGFR TKI treatment.
source: Non-genetic alterations, such as histological transformation from NSCLC to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), have also been reported in relapsed tumors (Sequist et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sequist et al., 2011

claim: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) has been reported in relapsed tumors after EGFR TKI treatment.
source: Non-genetic alterations, such as histological transformation from NSCLC to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), have also been reported in relapsed tumors (Sequist et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sequist et al., 2011

claim: Small subpopulations of cancer cells can evade lethal drug treatment by entering a drug tolerant 'persister' (DTP) state.
source: Furthermore, accumulating evidence has suggested that small subpopulations of cancer cells can evade lethal drug treatment by entering a drug tolerant 'persister' (DTP) state and serve as a founder for acquiring heterogeneous drug-resistance mechanisms upon long-term drug treatment (Sharma et al., 2010; Ramirez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sharma et al., 2010 and Ramirez et al., 2016

claim: A number of EGFR TKI-resistant tumours lack known resistance mechanisms.
source: Moreover, a number of EGFR TKI-resistant tumours lack known resistance mechanisms (Sequist et al., 2011), suggesting the existence of previously unrecognized mediators of EGFR TKI efficacy.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sequist et al., 2011

claim: HCC827 is a human NSCLC cell line harbouring activating EGFR mutation.
source: HCC827, a very commonly used EGFR-mutant NSCLC cell line, harbors ex19 del in EGFR and is highly sensitive to EGFR TKI treatment.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: HCC827 harbors ex19 del in EGFR.
source: HCC827, a very commonly used EGFR-mutant NSCLC cell line, harbors ex19 del in EGFR and is highly sensitive to EGFR TKI treatment.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: HCC827 is highly sensitive to EGFR TKI treatment.
source: HCC827, a very commonly used EGFR-mutant NSCLC cell line, harbors ex19 del in EGFR and is highly sensitive to EGFR TKI treatment.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: The IC50 of erlotinib for HCC827 cells after 3 days' exposure is 25.6 ± 3.6 nM.
source: Generation of a dose-response curve upon 3 days' erlotinib exposure yielded the IC50 25.6 ± 3.6 nM (Figure 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from dose-response curve shown in Figure 1A

claim: About 30% of HCC827 cells can survive initial pulse of high dose erlotinib (1 µM and above).
source: However, even with high dose of erlotinib (1 µM and above), about 30% of the cells could still survive this initial pulse (Figure 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from Figure 1A

claim: HCC827 cells are able to proliferate at a low rate when exposed to high dose of erlotinib (1 µM).
source: Examination of the cell proliferation in the presence of DMSO control or 1 µM erlotinib over a 30 day period using IncuCyte demonstrated that HCC827 cells were still able to proliferate at a low rate when exposed to high dose of erlotinib (Figure 1B).
evidence: Experimental data from IncuCyte assay shown in Figure 1B

claim: A small fraction of viable HCC827 cells exist after 9 days' erlotinib treatment, referred to as 'drug tolerant persister' (DTP) cells.
source: Additionally, colony formation assay also confirmed the existence of a small fraction of viable cells after 9 days' erlotinib treatment, referred to as 'drug tolerant persister' (DTP) cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assay shown in Figure 1C

claim: DTP cells commence cell proliferation in the presence of erlotinib, yielding colonies of cells referred to as 'drug tolerant expanded persister' (DTEP) cells or drug resistant cells.
source: Thereafter, the DTP cells commenced cell proliferation in the presence of erlotinib, yielding colonies of cells referred to as 'drug tolerant expanded persister' (DTEP) cells or drug resistant cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assay shown in Figure 1C

claim: The genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 screen used a pooled lentiviral sgRNA library targeting 18,360 genes with five sgRNAs per gene.
source: We introduced a pooled lentiviral single guide RNA (sgRNA) library targeting 18,360 genes (five sgRNAs per gene) into HCC827 cells with constitutive Cas9 expression (HCC827-Cas9) and treated these cells with DMSO or erlotinib.
evidence: Description of experimental methodology

claim: The CRISPR screen identified 35 genes whose inactivation caused sensitization to erlotinib in HCC827 cell line using stringent criteria (RSA ≤ −4 and Q1 z-score ≤ −1).
source: To identify high-confidence negatively selected hits, we used a stringent RSA ≤ −4 and Q1 z-score ≤ −1 threshold. This analysis identified 35 genes, the inactivation of which caused sensitization to erlotinib in HCC827 cell line (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: Experimental data from CRISPR screen shown in Figure 1E and supplementary files

claim: FGFR1 and YAP1 are known mediators of EGFR TKI resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
source: FGFR1 and YAP1, two known mediators of EGFR TKI resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC (Ware et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2016; Chaib et al., 2017; Ghiso et al., 2017), were among these hits.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ware et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2016; Chaib et al., 2017; Ghiso et al., 2017

claim: The 35 negatively selected genes from the CRISPR screen cluster into heparan sulfate metabolism, GPCR/G-protein signaling, Hippo-YAP signaling pathway, and components of the SAGA/transcriptional complex.
source: Mapping the 35-gene set on the STRING protein-protein interaction network and the Reactome database generated clusters consisting of heparan sulfate metabolism, GPCR/G-protein signaling, Hippo-YAP signaling pathway, as well as components of the SAGA/transcriptional complex (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), providing potential synthetic lethal partners with EGFR TKI in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
evidence: Bioinformatics analysis of screen hits shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: Using less stringent criteria (RSA ≤ −3 and Q1 z-score ≤ −1), 122 genes were identified whose loss sensitized HCC827 cells to erlotinib treatment.
source: A less stringent threshold (RSA ≤ −3 and Q1 z-score ≤ −1) generated a larger list of 122 genes whose loss sensitized HCC827 cells to erlotinib treatment (Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: Experimental data from CRISPR screen analysis

claim: The CRISPR screen identified 47 genes whose inactivation conferred resistance to erlotinib in HCC827 cell line using stringent criteria (RSA ≤ −4 and Q3 z-score ≥1).
source: Similarly, we applied a stringent RSA ≤ −4 and Q3 z-score ≥1 threshold to identify 47 genes whose inactivation conferred resistance to erlotinib in HCC827 cell line (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: Experimental data from CRISPR screen shown in Figure 1F and supplementary files

claim: Using less stringent criteria (RSA ≤ −3 and Q3 z-score ≥1), 171 genes were identified whose inactivation conferred resistance to erlotinib.
source: A less stringent threshold (RSA ≤ −3 and Q3 z-score ≥1) expanded the list to 171 genes (Supplementary file 1 and 2), including negative regulators of YAP signaling such as NF2/Merlin and SAV1, further warranting the importance of YAP signaling in mediating EGFR TKI resistance in lung cancer.
evidence: Experimental data from CRISPR screen analysis

claim: The 47 positively selected hits from the CRISPR screen enriched for PI3K-mTOR signaling and RAS-MAPK signaling pathways.
source: Protein network and pathway analyses of the 47 positively selected hits enriched for PI3K-mTOR signaling (such as PTEN, TSC1 and TSC2) and RAS-MAPK signaling (such as NF1, SPRY2 and LZTR1) pathways (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), two well-established modes of resistance to EGFR TKI in EGFR-mutant NSCLC (Pao and Chmielecki, 2010; Chong and Jänne, 2013; Niederst and Engelman, 2013; Rotow and Bivona, 2017), validating the good performance of our CRISPR screen.
evidence: Bioinformatics analysis of screen hits shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, supported by citations

claim: KEAP1 and FBXW7 loss have previously been shown to confer resistance to EGFR TKI treatment in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells.
source: Among them, we identified KEAP1 and FBXW7, the loss of which have previously been shown to confer resistance to EGFR TKI treatment in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells (Krall et al., 2017; Ye et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krall et al., 2017 and Ye et al., 2017

claim: Components of the Cullin 5 (CUL5)-RING E3 ligase (CRL5) complex (CUL5, RNF7 and UBE2F) and ARIH2 were positively selected hits in the CRISPR screen.
source: Interestingly, components of the Cullin 5 (CUL5)-RING E3 ligase (CRL5) complex (such as CUL5, RNF7 and UBE2F) as well as ARIH2, an Ariadne family RING-in-Between-RING (RBR) E3 ligase working together with CRL5, were amongst the positively selected hits, suggesting their previously unrecognized role in mediating EGFR TKI resistance in lung cancer.
evidence: Experimental data from CRISPR screen

claim: sgRNAs targeting YAP1, USP22, LPAR2, GNB2, PKN2 and RIC8A strongly sensitized HCC827 cells to both erlotinib and gefitinib treatment in colony formation assays.
source: Long-term colony formation assays confirmed that all sgRNAs targeting these genes strongly sensitized HCC827 cells to both erlotinib and gefitinib treatment (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assays shown in Figure 2B-C

claim: The synthetic lethal phenotype of negatively selected hits was similarly observed in NCI-H3255 cell line that expresses EGFR-L858R.
source: The synthetic lethal phenotype was similarly observed in another EGFR-mutant NSCLC cell line NCI-H3255 that expresses EGFR-L858R (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: sgRNAs targeting ARIH2, CUL5, RNF7, KCTD5, PDCD10 and BTAF1 demonstrated significant resistance to both erlotinib and gefitinib treatment in HCC827 cells.
source: Our results confirmed that all sgRNAs demonstrated significant resistance to both erlotinib and gefitinib treatment in HCC827 cells (Figure 2E–F) as well as in NCI-H3255 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assays shown in Figure 2E-F

claim: LPAR antagonists (Compound 2, AM095, and Ki16425) synergized with erlotinib to inhibit clonogenic cell growth in HCC827 and NCI-H3255 cells.
source: Indeed, colony formation assays in HCC827 and NCI-H3255 cells demonstrated that LPAR antagonists, such as Compound 2 (LPAR1 selective) (Qian et al., 2012), AM095 (LPAR1 selective) (Swaney et al., 2011) and Ki16425 (targeting LPAR1-3) (Ohta et al., 2003), synergized with erlotinib to inhibit clonogenic cell growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C, with citations for compound characterization

claim: RIC8A functions as a biosynthetic chaperone and guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for a subset of G protein α subunits.
source: RIC8A functions as a biosynthetic chaperone and guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for a subset of G protein α subunits (Nishimura et al., 2006; Gabay et al., 2011; Chan et al., 2013; Kant et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nishimura et al., 2006; Gabay et al., 2011; Chan et al., 2013; Kant et al., 2016

claim: RIC8A deficiency leads to loss of Gα subunits.
source: Previous study has shown that RIC8A deficiency leads to loss of Gα subunits, and consequently, Gβγ dimers dissociated from Gα subunits could be recognized by KCTD5 for degradation (Chishiki et al., 2013; Boularan et al., 2015; Brockmann et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chishiki et al., 2013; Boularan et al., 2015; Brockmann et al., 2017

claim: Gβγ dimers dissociated from Gα subunits could be recognized by KCTD5 for degradation.
source: Previous study has shown that RIC8A deficiency leads to loss of Gα subunits, and consequently, Gβγ dimers dissociated from Gα subunits could be recognized by KCTD5 for degradation (Chishiki et al., 2013; Boularan et al., 2015; Brockmann et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chishiki et al., 2013; Boularan et al., 2015; Brockmann et al., 2017

claim: RIC8A knockout in HCC827 cells leads to decreased protein abundance of Gαq (GNAQ) and Gβ2 (GNB2) subunits.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed RIC8A knockout efficiency and the consequent effect on the protein abundance of Gαq (GNAQ) and Gβ2 (GNB2) subunits as well as the on-target inhibition of EGFR and its downstream signaling upon erlotinib treatment (Figure 3A).
evidence: Experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 3A

claim: Cells deficient in RIC8A exhibited enhanced sensitivity to both erlotinib and gefitinib.
source: We then examined whether loss of RIC8A affects the overall EGFR TKI response in HCC827 cells by generating a dose-response curve. Cells deficient in RIC8A exhibited enhanced sensitivity to both erlotinib and gefitinib (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from dose-response curves shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: RIC8A depletion dramatically accelerated apoptosis induction by erlotinib, represented by increased caspase 3/7 activity.
source: Consistently, RIC8A depletion dramatically accelerated apoptosis induction by erlotinib, represented by the increased caspase 3/7 activity (Figure 3C).
evidence: Experimental data from caspase 3/7 activity assay shown in Figure 3C

claim: Loss of RIC8A had no effect on the basal proliferation of HCC827 cells.
source: Our results demonstrated that loss of RIC8A had no effect on the basal proliferation of HCC827 cells while dramatically suppressed erlotinib- and gefitinib-resistant colony formation (Figure 3D–E), which could be rescued by overexpression of CRISPR/Cas9-resistant RIC8A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assays shown in Figure 3D-E

claim: Loss of RIC8A dramatically suppressed erlotinib- and gefitinib-resistant colony formation in HCC827 cells.
source: Our results demonstrated that loss of RIC8A had no effect on the basal proliferation of HCC827 cells while dramatically suppressed erlotinib- and gefitinib-resistant colony formation (Figure 3D–E), which could be rescued by overexpression of CRISPR/Cas9-resistant RIC8A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assays shown in Figure 3D-E and rescue experiment in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Loss of RIC8A sensitized HCC4006 and PC9 cells (EGFR ex19 del) to EGFR TKI treatment.
source: Similar effects were also observed in two additional NSCLC cell lines with the same EGFR ex19 del, HCC4006 and PC9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–L).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–L

claim: Loss of RIC8A sensitized NCI-H3255 cells (EGFR-L858R) to EGFR TKI treatment and efficiently prevented erlotinib- and gefitinib-resistant colony formation.
source: Moreover, we also showed that loss of RIC8A sensitized cells to EGFR TKI treatment and efficiently prevented erlotinib- and gefitinib-resistant colony formation in NCI-H3255 cell line harboring EGFR-L858R mutation (Figure 3F–3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3F-3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: NCI-H1975 cells harbor EGFR-L858R and T790M mutations and are insensitive to erlotinib.
source: To investigate the potential role of RIC8A in mediating response to third-generation EGFR TKI, we deleted RIC8A in NCI-H1975 cells, which harbor EGFR-L858R and T790M mutations and thus insensitive to erlotinib (Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: Loss of RIC8A in NCI-H1975 cells dramatically enhanced the growth suppressive effect of EGF816.
source: Strikingly, loss of RIC8A in NCI-H1975 cells dramatically enhanced the growth suppressive effect (Figure 3L), promoted apoptosis (Figure 3M), and attenuated development of resistance (Figure 3N and O) upon EGF816 treatment.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3L-O

claim: Loss of RIC8A in NCI-H1975 cells promoted apoptosis upon EGF816 treatment.
source: Strikingly, loss of RIC8A in NCI-H1975 cells dramatically enhanced the growth suppressive effect (Figure 3L), promoted apoptosis (Figure 3M), and attenuated development of resistance (Figure 3N and O) upon EGF816 treatment.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3M

claim: Loss of RIC8A in NCI-H1975 cells attenuated development of resistance upon EGF816 treatment.
source: Strikingly, loss of RIC8A in NCI-H1975 cells dramatically enhanced the growth suppressive effect (Figure 3L), promoted apoptosis (Figure 3M), and attenuated development of resistance (Figure 3N and O) upon EGF816 treatment.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3N and O

claim: Loss of RIC8A exhibited no effect on the EGFR TKI sensitivity in EGFR wild-type (EGFR-WT) NSCLC cell lines (A549, NCI-1299 and NCI-H460) or normal human bronchial epithelial cell line BEAS-2B.
source: Moreover, loss of RIC8A exhibited no effect on the EGFR TKI sensitivity in EGFR wild-type (EGFR-WT) NSCLC cell lines (A549, NCI-1299 and NCI-H460) or normal human bronchial epithelial cell line BEAS-2B (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–P).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–P

claim: Loss of RIC8A is synthetic lethal with EGFR inhibition across a panel of NSCLC cell lines with various EGFR mutations.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that loss of RIC8A is synthetic lethal with EGFR inhibition across a panel of NSCLC cell lines with various EGFR mutations, representing a general mechanism.
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental results across different cell lines

claim: Gα protein coupled GPCR signaling modulates activities of Rho/Rac GTPase, which lead to actin cytoskeleton remodeling and regulate YAP signaling.
source: Gα protein coupled GPCR signaling has been well characterized to modulate activities of Rho/Rac GTPase, which in turn lead to actin cytoskeleton remodeling, consequently regulating YAP signaling via both LATS1/2-dependent and LATS1/2-independent mechanisms (Yu et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yu et al., 2012 and Ma et al., 2019

claim: Loss of RIC8A significantly decreased YAP reporter (GTIIC-GFP) activity in HEK293A cells.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first deleted RIC8A in HEK293A cells using two independent sgRNAs (Figure 4A) and verified that loss of RIC8A significantly decreased YAP reporter (GTIIC-GFP) activity (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), reduced expression of classical YAP target genes (ANKRD1, CTGF, and CYR61) (Figure 4C), and suppressed YAP-dependent growth of HEK293A cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from YAP reporter assay shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Loss of RIC8A reduced expression of classical YAP target genes (ANKRD1, CTGF, and CYR61) in HEK293A cells.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first deleted RIC8A in HEK293A cells using two independent sgRNAs (Figure 4A) and verified that loss of RIC8A significantly decreased YAP reporter (GTIIC-GFP) activity (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), reduced expression of classical YAP target genes (ANKRD1, CTGF, and CYR61) (Figure 4C), and suppressed YAP-dependent growth of HEK293A cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 4C

claim: Loss of RIC8A suppressed YAP-dependent growth of HEK293A cells.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first deleted RIC8A in HEK293A cells using two independent sgRNAs (Figure 4A) and verified that loss of RIC8A significantly decreased YAP reporter (GTIIC-GFP) activity (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), reduced expression of classical YAP target genes (ANKRD1, CTGF, and CYR61) (Figure 4C), and suppressed YAP-dependent growth of HEK293A cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assay shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: Defects resulting from RIC8A loss in HEK293A cells can be overcome by overexpression of constitutively active YAP (YAP-5SA).
source: Furthermore, these defects resulting from RIC8A loss can be overcome by overexpression of the constitutively active YAP (YAP-5SA) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Experimental data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D

claim: RIC8A positively regulates YAP signaling in HEK293A cells.
source: Together, these data strongly support the role of RIC8A in positively regulating YAP signaling in HEK293A cells.
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental results in HEK293A cells

claim: Loss of RIC8A resulted in an increase in YAP phosphorylation at Ser127 site across a panel of EGFR-mutant NSCLC cell lines.
source: Indeed, across a panel of EGFR-mutant NSCLC cell lines, loss of RIC8A resulted in an increase in YAP phosphorylation at Ser127 site, an indicator of YAP inactivation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Experimental data from Western blots shown in Figure 4D

claim: Loss of RIC8A significantly suppressed the expression of YAP target genes in all tested EGFR-mutant NSCLC cell lines.
source: In line with this finding, loss of RIC8A significantly suppressed the expression of YAP target genes in all tested cell lines (Figure 4E).
evidence: Experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 4E

claim: RIC8A positively regulates YAP signaling in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that RIC8A positively regulates YAP signaling in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells.
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental results in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells

claim: Overexpression of YAP-5SA in HCC827 cells blocked the effect of RIC8A loss on YAP signaling.
source: Moreover, overexpression of YAP-5SA in representative HCC827 cell line blocked the effect of RIC8A loss on YAP signaling (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G

claim: YAP activation conferred resistance to EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells.
source: Importantly, YAP activation itself conferred resistance to EGFR inhibition and blocked RIC8A loss-induced synthetic lethality with EGFR inhibition (Figure 4H–4J).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4H-4J

claim: YAP activation blocked RIC8A loss-induced synthetic lethality with EGFR inhibition.
source: Importantly, YAP activation itself conferred resistance to EGFR inhibition and blocked RIC8A loss-induced synthetic lethality with EGFR inhibition (Figure 4H–4J).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4H-4J

claim: Loss of RIC8A synergizes with EGFR inhibition by attenuating YAP signaling in lung cancer.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that loss of RIC8A synergizes with EGFR inhibition by attenuating YAP signaling in lung cancer.
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental results showing RIC8A regulation of YAP and effects on EGFR TKI sensitivity

claim: Loss of RHOA increased YAP phosphorylation at Ser127 site in HCC827 cells.
source: Indeed, loss of RHOA increased YAP phosphorylation at Ser127 site (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), decreased YAP-target gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), and induced synthetic lethality with EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: Loss of RHOA decreased YAP-target gene expression in HCC827 cells.
source: Indeed, loss of RHOA increased YAP phosphorylation at Ser127 site (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), decreased YAP-target gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), and induced synthetic lethality with EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: Loss of RHOA induced synthetic lethality with EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells.
source: Indeed, loss of RHOA increased YAP phosphorylation at Ser127 site (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), decreased YAP-target gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), and induced synthetic lethality with EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assay shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: RIC8A loss caused significant decrease in the expression of ARHGAP29.
source: In addition, ARHGAP29, encoding a Rho GTPase activating protein, was previously reported to be a YAP target gene (Qiao et al., 2017). We observed that RIC8A loss caused significant decrease in the expression of ARHGAP29 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F), which could provide a negative-feedback mechanism to alleviate the decrease of RHOA activity resulting from RIC8A loss.
evidence: Experimental data from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F, with citation to Qiao et al., 2017

claim: RIC8A loss caused morphological alteration in HCC827 cells.
source: Consistently, we observed a morphological alteration in HCC827 cells upon RIC8A loss (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G) and the decrease of Cofilin phosphorylation that is downstream of the RHOA-ROCK signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H), indicating that loss of RIC8A indeed negatively impacted the output from RHOA activation.
evidence: Experimental data from microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G

claim: RIC8A loss caused decrease of Cofilin phosphorylation that is downstream of the RHOA-ROCK signaling.
source: Consistently, we observed a morphological alteration in HCC827 cells upon RIC8A loss (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G) and the decrease of Cofilin phosphorylation that is downstream of the RHOA-ROCK signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H), indicating that loss of RIC8A indeed negatively impacted the output from RHOA activation.
evidence: Experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2H

claim: Treatment with Y-27632, the inhibitor of Rho-associated kinase ROCK, induced synthetic lethality with EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells.
source: Moreover, treatment with Y-27632, the inhibitor of Rho-associated kinase ROCK, also induced synthetic lethality with EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I–J).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assay shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2I–J

claim: The RIC8A-Gα-RHOA-YAP signaling axis is involved in the regulation of EGFR TKI sensitivity in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells.
source: Taken together, these data suggested the RIC8A-Gα-RHOA-YAP signaling axis is involved in the regulation of EGFR TKI sensitivity in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells.
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental results showing connections between RIC8A, RHOA, and YAP in regulating EGFR TKI sensitivity

claim: Loss of ARIH2 in HCC827 cells decreased sensitivity to erlotinib.
source: Loss of ARIH2 in HCC827 cells decreased sensitivity to erlotinib (Figure 5B) and reduced apoptosis induction upon erlotinib treatment (Figure 5C).
evidence: Experimental data from cell viability assay shown in Figure 5B

claim: Loss of ARIH2 in HCC827 cells reduced apoptosis induction upon erlotinib treatment.
source: Loss of ARIH2 in HCC827 cells decreased sensitivity to erlotinib (Figure 5B) and reduced apoptosis induction upon erlotinib treatment (Figure 5C).
evidence: Experimental data from caspase 3/7 activity assay shown in Figure 5C

claim: Loss of ARIH2 facilitated more HCC827 cells to enter into the DTP state.
source: To examine whether loss of ARIH2 could increase the reservoir of DTP cells, we treated control (sgAAVS) or ARIH2-deficient (sgARIH2) HCC827 cells with 1 µM of erlotinib or gefitinib for three rounds with each treatment lasting for 72 hr. Our results demonstrated that loss of ARIH2 facilitated more cells to enter into the DTP state (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: Experimental data from DTP assay shown in Figure 5D-E

claim: ARIH2 loss substantially enhanced clonogenic cell survival upon EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells.
source: To test long-term effects of ARIH2 loss, we first performed colony formation assays and confirmed that ARIH2 loss substantially enhanced clonogenic cell survival upon EGFR inhibition (Figure 5F–G), which could be rescued by overexpression of CRISPR/Cas9-resistant ARIH2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assays shown in Figure 5F-G and rescue experiment in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: ARIH2-deficient HCC827 cells showed substantial outgrowth under the pressure of EGFR inhibition in cell competition assay.
source: Next, we carried out a cell competition assay, in which unlabeled parental HCC827 cells were mixed in a ratio of 100:1 with RFP-labeled control or ARIH2-deficient cells and maintained in culture in the absence or presence of EGFR TKIs for three weeks (Figure 5H). Analysis of RFP-positive cells showed substantial outgrowth of the ARIH2-deficient cells under the pressure of EGFR inhibition (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: Experimental data from cell competition assay shown in Figure 5H-J

claim: Loss of ARIH2 has little or no effect on the basal proliferation of HCC827 cells.
source: The percentage of RFP-positive cells remained similarly in the absence of EGFR TKI (Figure 5I–J), together with no differential colony formation between control and ARIH2-deficient cells in the absence of EGFR TKI (Figure 5F–G), suggesting that loss of ARIH2 has little or no effect on the basal proliferation of HCC827 cells.
evidence: Inference from experimental data shown in Figure 5F-G and Figure 5I-J

claim: Drug resistance phenotype associated with ARIH2 loss was also observed in NCI-H3255 cell line.
source: Likewise, drug resistance phenotype associated with ARIH2 loss was also observed in NCI-H3255 cell line (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F

claim: ARIH2 loss had no effect on the EGFR TKI sensitivity in EGFR-WT NSCLC cells or normal cells.
source: On the contrast, ARIH2 loss had no effect on the EGFR TKI sensitivity in EGFR-WT NSCLC cells or normal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–P).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–P

claim: Loss of ARIH2 alone had little effect on tumor growth in the vehicle treatment group in HCC827 xenografts.
source: As shown in Figure 5K, loss of ARIH2 alone had little effect on tumor growth in the vehicle treatment group.
evidence: Experimental data from xenograft study shown in Figure 5K

claim: Erlotinib treatment efficiently suppressed tumor growth in control HCC827 xenografts, with resistance emerging after approximately 90 days of continuous erlotinib treatment.
source: Erlotinib treatment efficiently suppressed tumor growth (compared to vehicle treatment), with resistance emerging after approximately 90 days of continuous erlotinib treatment in control xenograft tumors (Figure 5K).
evidence: Experimental data from xenograft study shown in Figure 5K

claim: Loss of ARIH2 significantly accelerated the development of resistant tumors in HCC827 xenografts treated with erlotinib.
source: Importantly, loss of ARIH2 significantly accelerated the development of resistant tumors (Figure 5K–L).
evidence: Experimental data from xenograft study shown in Figure 5K-L

claim: Loss of ARIH2 confers resistance to EGFR inhibition in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
source: Taken together, these data further support the notion that loss of ARIH2 confers resistance to EGFR inhibition in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
evidence: Inference from multiple in vitro and in vivo experimental results

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified 46 proteins that significantly increased and 13 proteins that decreased upon ARIH2 loss in HCC827 cells.
source: Using a stringent criteria (|Log2 fold change| ≥ 0.9 and P value ≤ 0.001), we observed that 46 proteins significantly increased and 13 proteins decreased upon ARIH2 loss (Figure 6A).
evidence: Experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: Loss of ARIH2 increased protein levels of METAP2, ALDOA and PSAT1 in HCC827 cells without affecting their corresponding mRNA levels.
source: We first validated by immunoblotting analysis that loss of ARIH2 indeed increased protein levels of METAP2, ALDOA and PSAT1 in HCC827 cells (Figure 6B), without affecting their corresponding mRNA levels (Figure 6C), suggesting a possible post-transcriptional regulation mechanism.
evidence: Experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 6B and qRT-PCR shown in Figure 6C

claim: Loss of ARIH2 led to increase of METAP2 and ALDOA proteins, but not PSAT1 protein, in NCI-H3255 cells.
source: Loss of ARIH2 also led to increase of METAP2 and ALDOA proteins, but not PSAT1 protein, in NCI-H3255 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: Loss of ARIH2 or CUL5 dramatically increased protein abundance of METAP2, ALDOA and PSAT1 in HEK293T cells.
source: Moreover, loss of ARIH2 or CUL5 also dramatically increased protein abundance of METAP2, ALDOA and PSAT1 in HEK293T cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), suggesting a general mechanism of regulation of these proteins by ARIH2 and CUL5 complex.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: METAP2 overexpression confers resistance to EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells.
source: A long-term colony formation assay of the vector- and HA-METAP2-expressing HCC827 cells demonstrated that METAP2 overexpression confers resistance to EGFR inhibition (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assay shown in Figure 6E-F

claim: EGFR inhibition by erlotinib treatment drastically inhibited nascent protein synthesis in HCC827 cells.
source: EGFR inhibition by erlotinib treatment drastically inhibited nascent protein synthesis (Figure 6G), in line with its effect on overall growth inhibition.
evidence: Experimental data from AHA labeling shown in Figure 6G

claim: Cells with METAP2 overexpression exhibited increased protein synthesis compared to vehicle-expressing cells when challenged by erlotinib treatment.
source: Importantly, cells with METAP2 overexpression exhibited increased protein synthesis, compared to vehicle-expressing cells, when challenged by erlotinib treatment (Figure 6G).
evidence: Experimental data from AHA labeling shown in Figure 6G

claim: Loss of ARIH2 increased nascent protein synthesis upon EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells.
source: Furthermore, loss of ARIH2, which is able to increase METAP2 protein level, also increased nascent protein synthesis upon EGFR inhibition (Figure 6H).
evidence: Experimental data from AHA labeling shown in Figure 6H

claim: ARIH2 loss confers resistance to EGFR inhibition, at least in part, by maintaining higher protein synthesis rate through METAP2.
source: Together, these data suggest that ARIH2 loss confers resistance to EGFR inhibition, at least in part, by maintaining higher protein synthesis rate through METAP2.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing ARIH2 regulation of METAP2 and effects on protein synthesis and EGFR TKI resistance

claim: Proteasome inhibitor (Bortezomib) treatment increased METAP2 protein abundance in HCC827 cells.
source: Proteasome inhibitor (Bortezomib) treatment increased METAP2 protein abundance in HCC827 cells (Figure 6I), suggesting that METAP2 protein level is regulated by the proteasome-dependent degradation pathway.
evidence: Experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 6I

claim: Bortezomib induced METAP2 protein level increase was only observed in control cells but not in ARIH2-deficient cells.
source: Moreover, bortezomib induced METAP2 protein level increase was only observed in control cells but not in ARIH2-deficient cells (Figure 6J), indicating that proteasome-mediated METAP2 protein degradation is dependent on ARIH2.
evidence: Experimental data from Western blot shown in Figure 6J

claim: Loss of ARIH2 increased nascent METAP2 protein synthesis in HCC827 cells.
source: Specifically, we assessed de novo METAP2 protein synthesis in control or ARIH2-deficient HCC827 cells by AHA labeling followed by streptavidin pulldown and showed that loss of ARIH2 increased nascent METAP2 protein synthesis (Figure 6K), suggesting that ARIH2 indeed regulates METAP2 protein translation.
evidence: Experimental data from AHA labeling and pulldown shown in Figure 6K

claim: ARIH2 is capable of regulating both protein translation and protein degradation of METAP2.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that ARIH2 is capable of regulating both protein translation and protein degradation of METAP2.
evidence: Inference from multiple experimental results showing ARIH2 effects on METAP2 protein levels through different mechanisms

claim: Overexpression of ALDOA is capable to promote resistance to EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells.
source: Long-term colony formation assays showed that overexpression of ALDOA or PSAT1 is capable to promote resistance to EGFR inhibition (Figure 6M–N).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assay shown in Figure 6M-N

claim: Overexpression of PSAT1 is capable to promote resistance to EGFR inhibition in HCC827 cells.
source: Long-term colony formation assays showed that overexpression of ALDOA or PSAT1 is capable to promote resistance to EGFR inhibition (Figure 6M–N).
evidence: Experimental data from colony formation assay shown in Figure 6M-N

claim: Loss of ARIH2 confers resistance to EGFR inhibition in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells by integrating multiple mechanisms.
source: Thus, we concluded that loss of ARIH2 confers resistance to EGFR inhibition in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells by integrating multiple mechanisms.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing multiple proteins (METAP2, ALDOA, PSAT1) regulated by ARIH2 that contribute to resistance

claim: Previous studies employed siRNA or shRNA approaches or focused on small subsets of genes to identify genetic modifiers of EGFR TKI sensitivity.
source: Several studies have previously employed loss- or gain-of-function screens to profile genetic interactions with mutant EGFR in NSCLC cells to look for synthetic lethality (Bivona et al., 2011; de Bruin et al., 2014; Sharifnia et al., 2014; Lantermann et al., 2015; Liao et al., 2017). However, they utilized either small interfering RNA (siRNA) or short hairpin RNA (shRNA) approach or focused on small subsets of genes (such as tumor suppressors, oncogenes and genes encoding kinases), and identified distinct genetic modifiers of EGFR TKI sensitivity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bivona et al., 2011; de Bruin et al., 2014; Sharifnia et al., 2014; Lantermann et al., 2015; Liao et al., 2017

claim: LPAR signaling has been shown to contribute to malignancy and chemotherapy resistance in various tumors.
source: Interestingly, LPAR signaling has been shown to contribute to malignancy and chemotherapy resistance in various tumors (Yung et al., 2014; Hashimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yung et al., 2014 and Hashimoto et al., 2016

claim: LPAR signaling coupled with G12/13 has been shown to activate YAP pathway in HEK293A cells.
source: Interestingly, LPAR signaling coupled with G12/13 has been shown to activate YAP pathway in HEK293A cells (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 2012

claim: Majority of human uveal melanomas, driven by activating mutations in Gαq/11 proteins, depend on YAP signaling for tumorigenesis.
source: Moreover, majority of human uveal melanomas, driven by activating mutations in Gαq/11 proteins, depend on YAP signaling for tumorigenesis (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 2014

claim: Ric-8A gene deletion significantly suppressed tumorigenesis in a mouse model of oncogenic Gαq-driven melanoma.
source: Ric-8A gene deletion significantly suppressed tumorigenesis in a mouse model of oncogenic Gαq-driven melanoma (Patel and Tall, 2016), implying its regulation of YAP signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by citation to Patel and Tall, 2016

claim: YAP signaling pathway has been shown to mediate resistance to RAF and MEK inhibition.
source: YAP signaling pathway has also been shown to mediate resistance to other targeted therapies, such as RAF and MEK inhibition (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2015

claim: Reduced NF1 (neurofibromin) expression has been observed in clinical specimens with acquired resistance to EGFR TKI treatment.
source: On the other hand, reduced NF1 (neurofibromin) expression (de Bruin et al., 2014) or loss of PTEN (Sos et al., 2009) has been observed in clinical specimens with acquired resistance to EGFR TKI treatment.
evidence: Supported by citation to de Bruin et al., 2014

claim: Loss of PTEN has been observed in clinical specimens with acquired resistance to EGFR TKI treatment.
source: On the other hand, reduced NF1 (neurofibromin) expression (de Bruin et al., 2014) or loss of PTEN (Sos et al., 2009) has been observed in clinical specimens with acquired resistance to EGFR TKI treatment.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sos et al., 2009

claim: ARIH2 (TRIAD1) is a member of the RING-in-between-RING (RBR) E3 ubiquitin ligase family.
source: ARIH2 (also known as TRIAD1), a member of the RING-in-between-RING (RBR) E3 ubiquitin ligase family (Dove and Klevit, 2017), binds to and is activated specifically by activated CRL5 complex (Kelsall et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dove and Klevit, 2017

claim: ARIH2 binds to and is activated specifically by activated CRL5 complex.
source: ARIH2 (also known as TRIAD1), a member of the RING-in-between-RING (RBR) E3 ubiquitin ligase family (Dove and Klevit, 2017), binds to and is activated specifically by activated CRL5 complex (Kelsall et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelsall et al., 2013

claim: ARIH2 is essential for embryogenesis.
source: ARIH2 is essential for embryogenesis and has been shown to modulate inflammatory responses (Lin et al., 2013; Kawashima et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2013 and Kawashima et al., 2017

claim: ARIH2 has been shown to modulate inflammatory responses.
source: ARIH2 is essential for embryogenesis and has been shown to modulate inflammatory responses (Lin et al., 2013; Kawashima et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2013 and Kawashima et al., 2017

claim: CUL5 deficiency has been shown to promote SCLC metastasis by stabilizing integrin β1.
source: For instance, CUL5 deficiency has been shown to promote SCLC metastasis by stabilizing integrin β1 (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2019

claim: CRL5 complex plays important roles in modulating multiple aspects of the cellular response to heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) inhibition.
source: Additionally, CRL5 complex also plays important roles in modulating multiple aspects of the cellular response to heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) inhibition (Samant et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Samant et al., 2014

claim: METAP2 has been shown to be involved in NSCLC.
source: Through a proteomics study, we identified METAP2 (methionine aminopeptidase 2), a protein that has been shown to be involved in NSCLC (Shimizu et al., 2016), the abundance of which was dramatically increased upon ARIH2 loss.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shimizu et al., 2016

claim: The genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen revealed both known and potential synthetic lethal vulnerabilities with EGFR TKI as well as modes of resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
source: Together, our genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function genetic screen successfully revealed both known and potential synthetic lethal vulnerabilities with EGFR TKI as well as modes of resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
evidence: Summary statement based on the entire screen results

claim: Knockout of RIC8A enhanced EGFR TKI-induced cell death.
source: We show that knockout of RIC8A, essential for G-alpha protein activation, enhanced EGFR TKI-induced cell death.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study

claim: RIC8A is a positive regulator of YAP signaling.
source: Mechanistically, we demonstrate that RIC8A is a positive regulator of YAP signaling, activation of which rescued the EGFR TKI sensitizing phenotype resulting from RIC8A knockout.
evidence: Summary of mechanistic findings from the study

claim: Activation of YAP signaling rescued the EGFR TKI sensitizing phenotype resulting from RIC8A knockout.
source: Mechanistically, we demonstrate that RIC8A is a positive regulator of YAP signaling, activation of which rescued the EGFR TKI sensitizing phenotype resulting from RIC8A knockout.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study

claim: Knockout of ARIH2 or other components in the Cullin-5 E3 complex conferred resistance to EGFR inhibition.
source: We also show that knockout of ARIH2, or other components in the Cullin-5 E3 complex, conferred resistance to EGFR inhibition, in part by promoting nascent protein synthesis through METAP2.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study

claim: ARIH2 knockout confers resistance to EGFR inhibition in part by promoting nascent protein synthesis through METAP2.
source: We also show that knockout of ARIH2, or other components in the Cullin-5 E3 complex, conferred resistance to EGFR inhibition, in part by promoting nascent protein synthesis through METAP2.
evidence: Summary of mechanistic findings from the study
